newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - July 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - July 17.

text.p: Following are the highlights of the Irish press on Thursday:
- Irish prime minister Bertie Ahern has conceded the principle that a second tribunal will have to be established to further investigate Charles Haughey's financial affairs while he was in office.
- The European Commission has pledged to open membership talks with six more states, signalling an end to the one billion a year structural funding which Ireland currently enjoys.
- Two men were charged yesterday with the capital murder of detective Jerry McCabe last year.
- The Stormont talks on Northern Ireland reach a critical juncture with the coming six days set to determine whether a new ceasefire is in prospect.
- More than 80 percent of burglaries, muggings and thefts from cars in Dublin which lead to charges are carried out by drug abusers, according to new research.
- Tony O'Reilly is a billionaire, according to the U.S. business magazine Forbes which includes him in its new list of the world's 200 richest people.
- Food prices will fall and aid for small farmers will be increased under the new EU farm policy announced yesterday but the 36 billion plan could penalise bigger farmers.

- New problems loomed on three fronts for Charles Haughey last night as he faces two internal Fianna Fail investigations into his finances and a second, more broadly based tribunal of inquiry which will be set up after the McCracken report is published in August.

- Unionists walked out of the multi-party talks on the North's future last night after failing to get the clarification they had demanded on the government's proposals for the handing over of IRA weapons.

- Forbairt, the state body responsible for indigenous industry, turned in a strong job creation performance over the last 18 months and is now confident its 1999 target of 12,000 net new jobs will be achieved two years early.
- Allied Irish Banks value on the stock market soared through the five billion barrier yesterday - the first time that an Irish company has achieved such a high capitalisation.
- The biggest probe into the political system in the history of the state will be launched after the publication of the McCracken payments to politicians inquiry next month.
- Ireland's booming economy could he heading for a serious slowdown with confirmation that EU regional and farm aid, worth 2.2 billion a year, is to be slashed.

- Irish Continental Group and Mersey Docks and Harbour Co have lodged a joint bid for the Bell Mertens terminal in Rotterdam belonging to Waterford-based Bell Lines which went into liquidation last week.
